extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous Victorian sketches / general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and qualities for composing short, humorous observational sketches that rely on character detail, anecdote, satire, and comic narrator voice (as exemplified by Dickens' sketches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through vivid physical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of concise, specific physical and costume details to create instantly recognisable comic characters (e.g., 'a brown-whiskered, white-hatted, no-coated cabman; his nose was generally red; ... his neck was usually garnished with a bright yellow handkerchief').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide small, striking particulars (hat, handkerchief, boot style, flower/straw in mouth) that convey personality at a glance; place them early and repeat or recall them for comic recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration / hyperbolic ubiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplify presence or effect of an object or person for comic force (e.g., the red cab is described as 'omnipresent' and everywhere 'bumping up against the posts' and contriving impossible entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assert large-scale consequences or ubiquity (the object 'everywhere', the action 'could have contrived to get into at all') to create absurdity; avoid literalism—the humour depends on overstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantomime and physical-comedy description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe bodily action and stage-like gestures in a slightly theatrical register: 'The getting into a cab is ... essentially melodramatic' with a step-by-step 'ballet' of movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down a small everyday action into comic, almost choreographed stages; rhythm and precise verbs (dart, bound, bend, knock) heighten the visual humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdote plus sequel
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell a short comic incident and explicitly supply its sequel to complete the joke ('A story is nothing without the sequel; and therefore, we may state...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't leave punchlines unresolved—follow up the immediate gag with consequences or an ironic aftermath (prison, singing in solitary) to amplify comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-earnest narrator voice and asides
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a voice that feigns seriousness or administrative tone while making sly comments ('We hope our readers will not be alarmed at this rather ominous title... we are not about to become political').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parenthetical remarks, rhetorical questions, and modest disclaimers to create rapport and ironic distance; the narrator's persona is a key source of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire by social-contrast and inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose institutional or social dignity as ridiculous by juxtaposing high office with petty behaviour (Magistracy 'in ecstasies' at a cabman's humour; Members lounging, shouting, and dining).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight incongruity between expected decorum and observed folly; let the target's self-importance be the butt of the joke rather than crude insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and catalogue for rhythmic comic piling-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Use serial lists and piling of items to produce a comic cadence (e.g., 'hackney-coaches, and drays, and carts, and waggons, and omnibuses').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition and cumulative cataloguing to overwhelm the reader and create comedic momentum; vary length and punctuation for tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialect and phonetic spelling for character voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Render speech with nonstandard spelling and colloquial forms to convey class/region and comic tone ('Wery good; that'll bring me up to the middle o' next month', 'O'ny a cab, sir').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ measured dialect features to characterise without caricaturing beyond recognition; balance readability with authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy through purposeful omission / mock-parliamentary pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline to narrate needless factual minutiae ('Mr. William Barker was born—but why need we relate where Mr. William Barker was born, or when?') to comedic effect and to maintain pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deliberate withholding or parenthetical dismissal to mock excessive detail and to keep focus on the humorous core; this also parodies formal record-keeping or official prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal types and archetypes as comic shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Populate sketches with recognisable social types (the county Member, militia-officer, hereditary bondsman, the butler Nicholas) so that a few traits suffice to produce laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a few salient traits per archetype (dress, gesture, habitual phrase) so readers immediately slot them into a satirical category; mix types for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironical moralising / wry generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn an observed detail into a small ironic maxim or social observation ('people are content to pay handsomely for excitement; where can it be procured at a cheaper rate?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After describing a comic scene, deliver a pithy, slightly knowing generalisation that reframes the scene and elicits a smile rather than didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-like set pieces and scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a theatrical, sensory environment (strewed trunks, uprooted post, crowd 'cooling their flushed faces against the glass windows of a chemist’s shop') that primes the comic incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor a joke in a vividly drawn locale; sensory detail makes the absurdity plausible and heightens the comic payoff when action occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small gestures as recurring comic motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat or recall minor habits (the cabman's straw/flower, Nicholas's judgement of cheese, the militia-officer's 'He-ar-He-ar') as running gags to reward reader recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce motifs early and echo them; repetition builds familiarity and can convert a small detail into a comic motif.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic timing via pacing and controlled digression
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance brief digressions and return to the main thread (e.g., long digressions on Mr. Barker's past then back to omnibus anecdotes) to control suspense and deliver punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asides and parenthetical commentary sparingly to tease readers; the return to the main narrative should feel like a setup/ payoff structure—delay can sharpen humour, but overlong wandering deflates it.
